# Results — Study 395 (Quantum-Computing-Basket)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The "quantum-computing basket" (IONQ,
RGTI, QBTS, QUBT) — the four pure-play quantum names — held equal-weight, monthly-rebalanced, and
raced against the market (SPY), the tech tape (QQQ), and the **diversified** quantum ETF (QTUM).
We split the "next big thing" claim in two: is the spectacular headline return a **real,
risk-adjusted edge**, or a **high-volatility hype cycle** whose raw CAGR evaporates the moment you
look at Sharpe, drawdown, and the standard error of the spread? Offline & deterministic from the
cache; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance monthly **total return** (auto-adjusted closes, public, no key) |
| Window | **2021-05 → 2026-05** (61 complete months; ≈ 5.1 years) |
| Basket | **4** pure-plays: IONQ (trapped-ion), RGTI (superconducting), QBTS (annealing), QUBT (photonic) |
| Controls | QTUM (diversified ~70-name quantum ETF) · SPY (market) · QQQ (tech tape) |
| Costs | 10 bps one-way × turnover per monthly rebalance |
| Panel fingerprint | `d955f566bc4b` |

> **Scope caveats (named on the axes).** *Signal* — the four pure-plays are the **surviving**
> de-SPAC cohort that made it to a listing; the many quantum SPACs that delisted or never priced
> are absent (survivorship — a bias that runs **bullish**). The window starts **2021-05** because
> that is the first month all four trade (the basket does not exist earlier), so this is **one
> short regime** (≈5.1 years, a single speculative-tech cycle). *Tradability* — a 160%-vol,
> −84%-drawdown sleeve is not a NAV-scale holding regardless of its point CAGR.

## Half 1 — the raw CAGR is spectacular (this is the hook)

Equal-weight, monthly-rebalanced; CAGR / annualised Sharpe / annualised vol / max drawdown over the
61 months.

| leg | CAGR | Sharpe | ann vol | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Quantum basket (4 pure-plays)** | **+59.1%** | **0.75** | **160%** | **−84.3%** |
| QTUM ETF (diversified quantum) | +27.9% | **1.06** | 27% | −34.5% |
| S&P 500 (SPY) | +13.9% | 0.91 | 16% | −23.9% |
| Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) | +17.3% | 0.88 | 21% | −32.6% |
| Basket, net of 10 bps one-way costs | +58.9% | 0.74 | — | — |

A **+59%/yr** CAGR against the market's **+14%/yr** is the entire "next big thing" pitch — and it is
*real* on this tape. But read the next two columns. The basket carries a **160% annualised
volatility** and an **−84% peak-to-trough drawdown**, so its **Sharpe is 0.75 — *below* the S&P
500's 0.91**, and less than *three-quarters* of the diversified QTUM ETF's **1.06**. The big number
is bought entirely with risk: per unit of volatility the basket *underperforms* the index it claims
to leave behind, and costs (net Sharpe 0.74) are a rounding error next to the risk.

## Half 2 — the spread is not statistically significant (the standard error)

HAC (Newey-West) t-stat of the basket's monthly spread. Both legs are fully invested, so the raw
difference *is* the excess-of-each-other return.

| spread | mean | HAC t | n |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Basket − SPY | **+104.6%/yr** | **1.23** | 61 |
| Basket − QQQ | +100.8%/yr | 1.19 | 61 |
| Basket − QTUM | +90.8%/yr | 1.12 | 61 |

The spread's *point estimate* is enormous, but its **standard error is enormous too**: at **HAC
t = 1.23 vs SPY** (and 1.19 vs QQQ, 1.12 vs the diversified ETF) it **fails the t ≥ 2 bar**. A
+100%/yr "edge" that a Newey-West *t* can't separate from zero is not an edge — it is a few violent
up-months (the 2024-2025 quantum melt-up) inside a tape of −90%-class drawdowns. The outperformance
is statistically indistinguishable from a high-variance coin landing heads over one short regime.

## Is it a broad theme or a few moon-shots? — single-name decomposition

HAC t of each member's monthly excess over SPY, with its own risk stats.

| name | CAGR | ann vol | max drawdown | excess / yr | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| IONQ | +45.3% | 117% | −86% | +76.8% | 1.40 |
| QBTS | +24.4% | 174% | −95% | +105.2% | 1.27 |
| RGTI | +20.4% | 218% | −96% | +119.4% | 1.11 |
| QUBT | +14.1% | 260% | −95% | +117.1% | 0.90 |

**Not one of the four clears t = 2 individually** — and every one has a **−86% to −96% drawdown**
and a **triple-digit** annualised volatility. This is the signature of a lottery cohort, not a
factor: each name's CAGR is a survivor's tale (the ones that *didn't* round-trip to zero aren't in
the basket), and none of them, alone or pooled, produces a spread the inference can certify.

## Synthetic positive control — risk + small samples defeat the spread

A deterministic monthly panel (fixed seed, 60 months × 5 names) where a *hype basket* of high-beta,
fat-tailed names is planted with a controllable **risk-adjusted** edge (`edge_sharpe`). At
`edge_sharpe = 0` each hype name has **zero** expected excess over the market — the fat volatility
only inflates the noise — so a *forward-nameable* basket has no significant spread however large a
lucky-draw CAGR looks. A planted Sharpe edge must light the HAC *t* up.

| planted edge | basket CAGR | Sharpe | spread vs market / yr | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `edge_sharpe = 0.0` (NO true edge) | −10.6% | 0.23 | +4.7%/yr | **0.18** |
| `edge_sharpe = 1.0` (real edge) | +256.5% | 2.05 | +146.9%/yr | **5.71** |

The null row is decisive: with **zero** true risk-adjusted edge the basket's spread sits at
**t = 0.18** — a fat-tailed basket cannot manufacture a significant HAC *t* out of pure beta-plus-
noise (across 20 seeds the null *t* averages −0.11 and crosses 2 once, ≈ the nominal 5% rate). Only
a genuine **+1.0 Sharpe** edge drives *t* to 5.71. The engine is faithful: it certifies a spread
*only* where a risk-adjusted edge is planted — which is exactly why the real-tape *t* of **1.23**
reads as **absence of a certifiable edge**, not proof of one.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The raw basket-minus-SPY spread is huge (**+104.6%/yr**) but **fails the t ≥ 2
  bar** (HAC **t = 1.23**, n = 61; 1.19 vs QQQ, 1.12 vs the diversified ETF), and **no single name
  clears t = 2** either. The basket's **Sharpe (0.75) is *below* the market's (0.91)** and far
  below the diversified QTUM ETF's (1.06): the spectacular number is bought entirely with
  volatility, not skill. Add the survivorship of the de-SPAC cohort and the single short regime, and
  a positive-but-insignificant, risk-unrewarded point estimate ⇒ `WEAK`, not `REAL`.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Costs are trivial (net Sharpe 0.74 vs 0.75 gross). What kills it is
  **risk**: a **160% annualised volatility** and an **−84% drawdown** (individual names −86% to
  −96%) make the basket un-allocatable at any NAV scale — and on a risk-adjusted basis it *loses* to
  both SPY and the QTUM ETF you could actually have bought from day one. The +59%/yr is a number you
  could not have held through the −84% draw, and were not paid to take.
- **Next big thing? — HYPE-CYCLE.** The "ride the quantum revolution" trade is, on the only tape we
  have, a **high-variance lottery dressed as a thesis**: a real technology with no profits yet,
  whose stock cohort delivers a giant CAGR, a giant drawdown, a sub-market Sharpe, and a HAC *t* that
  can't reach significance. The diversified ETF (Sharpe 1.06) is the only risk-rewarded way to
  "play quantum" here — and even it is not a free lunch. Same thematic-basket family as
  [Study 393 (AI-Datacenter-Basket)](../393-ai-datacenter-basket/) and
  [Study 334 (ARK-Innovation)](../334-ark-innovation/); there the critique is ex-post selection,
  here it is risk and sample size.

> **One-line.** The quantum-computing basket really did return +59%/yr vs the market's +14% — but
> it did so at 160% volatility with an −84% drawdown, a Sharpe (0.75) *below* the S&P 500's, and a
> HAC *t* of 1.23 that can't separate the spread from zero; strip the hype and you're left with a
> survivorship-tilted lottery over one short regime that a synthetic null reproduces from pure
> beta-plus-noise (t = 0.18), while the diversified QTUM ETF (Sharpe 1.06) quietly does the theme
> better. Real raw return, no certifiable edge, undeployable as a holding — a hype cycle, not the
> next big thing.
